--- title: "R Package Tutorial: tipr" --- # Introduction - **tipr** performs *tipping-point sensitivity analyses* for unmeasured confounding: it solves for the strength of a hypothetical confounder that would move an observed estimate to the null (or any chosen reference value). [R Causal](https://r-causal.github.io/tipr/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - **Key functions covered here** - `tip()`, `tip_with_binary()` – generic continuous / binary confounder engines. - Scale-specific wrappers: `tip_or()`, `tip_rr()`, `tip_hr()`, `tip_coef()` and their `_with_binary`, `_with_r2` variants. - **Typical use-cases** - Post-hoc robustness checks for observational studies. - Sensitivity reporting in clinical-trial subgroup or per-protocol analyses. - Pre-analysis planning (how strong must lurking confounding be to matter?). - **Benefits vs. alternatives** - Can target *any* effect scale (OR, RR, HR, β). - Integrates cleanly with `broom` output pipes and plotting tools (unlike **EValue**, which returns scalars, or **sensemakr**, which focuses on partial $R^2$). - Offers quick grid evaluations useful for interactive dashboards. [Journal of Open Source Software](https://joss.theoj.org/papers/10.21105/joss.04495?utm_source=chatgpt.com) ## Getting Started ::: {.cell} ::: ## A First “Hello tipr” ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display}
| effect_adjusted| effect_observed| exposure_confounder_effect| confounder_outcome_effect| n_unmeasured_confounders| |---------------:|---------------:|--------------------------:|-------------------------:|------------------------:| | 1| 1.5| 0.4| 2.755676| 1|
::: ::: Interpretation: **If** an unmeasured *continuous* confounder raised the outcome hazard by the returned HR (≈ 2.8), *and* was associated with exposure via HR = 0.40, the observed HR would shrink to 1 (no effect). ### Scaffold-Yourself Exercise 1. Change the `exposure_confounder_effect` to 0.10, 0.20, … 1.00. 2. Record the required confounder–outcome HR each time. 3. Plot and describe the trend. # Conceptual Foundations ### What Is a “Tipping Point”? A tipping point is the set of confounder parameters $(\gamma_{UX},\ \gamma_{UY})$ that exactly *cancels* the bias in an observed effect $\hat\theta$. Algebraically we solve $$ \theta_\text{obs} = \theta_\text{true}\times\operatorname{Bias}(\gamma_{UX},\gamma_{UY}), $$ then set $\theta_\text{true}=1$ (null) and invert. For linear models the bias is additive; for ratio scales it is multiplicative. ### DAG Perspective (drawn with `dagitty` + `ggdag`) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Minimal DAG for tipping-point logic: U confounds the X→Y relation.](tipr_files/figure-html/dag-basic-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: **Nuance:** *tipr* assumes *single* unmeasured confounder $U$. Multiple moderate confounders are equivalent to one composite confounder with aggregated effects—a useful but sometimes overlooked approximation. # Key Functions and Features Below each function appears twice: a **basic** and an **advanced** example, followed by tips and contrasts. ## 1. `tip()` – Continuous $U$ on Any Linear-Coefficient Scale ### Detailed Explanation `tip()` targets estimates on *additive* scales (e.g., linear-regression coefficients). It requires the observed coefficient and *either* the exposure–confounder effect or the confounder–outcome effect; it returns the unknown partner. **Syntax** ```r tip(effect_observed, exposure_confounder_effect = NULL, confounder_outcome_effect = NULL) ``` ### Basic Example – Body-Mass vs. Blood Pressure ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display}
| effect_adjusted| effect_observed| exposure_confounder_effect| confounder_outcome_effect| n_unmeasured_confounders| |---------------:|---------------:|--------------------------:|-------------------------:|------------------------:| | 1| 2| 0.3| 10.07937| 1|
::: ::: ### Advanced Example – High-Dimensional Simulation ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display}
| effect_adjusted| effect_observed| exposure_confounder_effect| confounder_outcome_effect| n_unmeasured_confounders| |---------------:|---------------:|--------------------------:|-------------------------:|------------------------:| | 1| 1.522675| -1.884298| 0.8| 1|
::: ::: ### Tips, Nuances, Misconceptions - **Linearity**: bias formula derives from linear expectation; use with log-transformed outcomes for skewed data. - **Common misconception**: A large required γ_UY means “safe.” Not necessarily—plausibility depends on domain knowledge. - **Contrast:** **sensemakr** computes *partial $R^2$* needed; *tipr* computes effect size directly, often easier to interpret in applied biomedical terms. ## 2. `tip_with_binary()` – Binary $U$ ### Detailed Explanation Adapts Cornfield conditions: specify two of `exposed_confounder_prev`, `unexposed_confounder_prev`, `confounder_outcome_effect`. ### Basic Example – Smoking (U) in Diet-Heart Study ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display}
| effect_adjusted| effect_observed| exposed_confounder_prev| unexposed_confounder_prev| confounder_outcome_effect| n_unmeasured_confounders| |---------------:|---------------:|-----------------------:|-------------------------:|-------------------------:|------------------------:| | 1| 1.4| 0.25| 0.05| 3.222222| 1|
::: ::: ### Advanced Example – Sensitivity Grid ::: {#tbl-tip-bin-adv .cell tbl-cap='Grid of required confounder–outcome effects over varying prevalences.'} ::: {.cell-output-display}
| exp_prev| unexp_prev| gamma_UY| |--------:|----------:|----------:| | 0.1| 0.01| 5.651163| | 0.2| 0.01| 3.150538| | 0.3| 0.01| 2.398601| | 0.4| 0.01| 2.036269| | 0.5| 0.01| 1.823045| | 0.1| 0.04| 10.090909| | 0.2| 0.04| 3.777778| | 0.3| 0.04| 2.639344| | 0.4| 0.04| 2.162791| | 0.5| 0.04| 1.900901| | 0.1| 0.07| 201.000000| | 0.2| 0.07| 4.921569| | 0.3| 0.07| 2.980198| | 0.4| 0.07| 2.324503| | 0.5| 0.07| 1.995025| | 0.1| 0.10| NA| | 0.2| 0.10| 7.666667| | 0.3| 0.10| 3.500000| | 0.4| 0.10| 2.538461| | 0.5| 0.10| 2.111111| | 0.1| 0.13| NA| | 0.2| 0.13| 23.222222| | 0.3| 0.13| 4.389831| | 0.4| 0.13| 2.834862| | 0.5| 0.13| 2.257862| | 0.1| 0.16| NA| | 0.2| 0.16| NA| | 0.3| 0.16| 6.263158| | 0.4| 0.16| 3.272727| | 0.5| 0.16| 2.449275| | 0.1| 0.19| NA| | 0.2| 0.19| NA| | 0.3| 0.19| 12.764706| | 0.4| 0.19| 3.985075| | 0.5| 0.19| 2.709402|
::: ::: ### What happens here 1. **`possibly()`** ```r safe_tip <- possibly(.f, otherwise = NA_real_) ``` Wraps your original anonymous function so that if it ever errors (i.e. the prevalence difference is too small), you quietly get `NA_real_` instead of stopping. 2. **`map2_dbl()`** Applies `safe_tip(exp_prev[i], unexp_prev[i])` for each row and always returns a **numeric** vector (with `NA`s where the underlying call failed). 3. **Result** Your `prev_grid$gamma_UY` will now be a length-15 numeric vector. Whenever `tip_gamma()` can’t find a valid confounder (as in your index 16 error), you’ll see an `NA` there rather than a hard stop. Visualize: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](tipr_files/figure-html/tip-bin-heat-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Nuances & Compare - **Rare U assumption**: When `unexposed_confounder_prev≃0`, results mimic classical Cornfield inequality. - **Contrast**: **EValue** provides a single minimal RR needed under *equal* prevalence—*tipr* lets prevalences differ, giving richer scenarios. ## 3. Scale-Specific Wrappers (`tip_or()`, `tip_rr()`, `tip_hr()`) ### Detailed Explanation These thin wrappers set default link transformers and interpretation messages. `tip_hr()` offers an **`hr_correction`** argument for common outcomes (>15 %) to adjust the risk-ratio approximation [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/tipr/versions/1.0.2/topics/tip_hr?utm_source=chatgpt.com). ### Basic Example – Odds Ratio ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display}
| effect_adjusted| effect_observed| exposure_confounder_effect| confounder_outcome_effect| n_unmeasured_confounders| |---------------:|---------------:|--------------------------:|-------------------------:|------------------------:| | 1| 2.1| 0.3| 11.85944| 1|
::: ::: ### Advanced Example – Hazard Ratio with Correction ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display}
| effect_adjusted| effect_observed| exposure_confounder_effect| confounder_outcome_effect| n_unmeasured_confounders| |---------------:|---------------:|--------------------------:|-------------------------:|------------------------:| | 1| 1.38397| 0.4| 2.253288| 1|
::: ::: ### Nuances - **HR Correction**: For cumulative incidences >15 %, hazard ratios diverge from risk ratios—enable `hr_correction`. - **Misconception**: Setting *both* `exposure_confounder_effect` *and* `confounder_outcome_effect` will *always* error; but if both are supplied, the function reports how many such confounders would be needed to tip (nice diagnostic!). ## 4. Partial $R^2$ Variants (`*_with_r2`) ### Detailed Explanation Instead of effect sizes, specify the *partial $R^2$* that $U$ explains in *X* and *Y*. Helpful when domain experts think in %-variance terms. ### Example – Robustness Value ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display}
| effect_adjusted| lb_adjusted| ub_adjusted| effect_observed| lb_observed| ub_observed| se_observed| df_observed| confounder_exposure_r2| confounder_outcome_r2| |---------------:|-----------:|-----------:|---------------:|-----------:|-----------:|-----------:|-----------:|----------------------:|---------------------:| | 0| -0.176947| 0.176947| 0.25| 0.1508014| 0.3491986| 0.05| 100| 0.7142857| 0.1|
::: ::: ### Compare vs. **sensemakr** `sensemakr` computes “robustness value” via $R^2$; *tipr* adds direct solver so you can toggle between effect-size and variance descriptions seamlessly. # Common Workflows & In-Depth Examples ## Basic Workflow (Logistic Regression) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display}
| effect_adjusted| effect_observed| exposure_confounder_effect| confounder_outcome_effect| n_unmeasured_confounders| |---------------:|---------------:|--------------------------:|-------------------------:|------------------------:| | 1| 1.036921| 0.2| 1.198748| 1|
::: ::: ## Intermediate Workflow – Continuous vs. Binary $U$ Side-by-Side 1. Run `tip()` with realistic continuous $γ_{UX} = 0.3$. 2. Run `tip_with_binary()` under plausible prevalences. 3. Plot both required $γ_{UY}$ values to compare robustness. ## Advanced Workflow – Interactive Grid + DAG Overlay ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](tipr_files/figure-html/wf-adv-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Interpret the intersection where plausible $γ_{UX}$ meets required γ_UY. If intersection lies above typical U effects, the estimate is robust. ## Advanced Features & Customization - **Vectorized calls**: pass vectors to `effect_observed` for batch analyses. - **Integration**: because outputs are numeric, you can feed them into **shiny** dashboards for real-time robustness sliders. - **Large datasets**: no raw data are needed—only summary estimates—making *tipr* trivially memory-safe. ## Troubleshooting and FAQs | Symptom | Diagnosis | Fix | |---------|-----------|-----| | “unused argument” | Called `tip_with_binary` without parentheses | Add `()` or ensure all required args | | Infinite output | Requested impossible combination (e.g., $γ_{UX} = 0$) | Use realistic non-zero $γ_{UX}$ or check input order | | Negative required effect | Swapped sign on `exposure_confounder_effect` | Remember: log-ratio <0 means protective confounder | ## Best Practices - **Triangulate**: report *tipr* alongside **EValue** and **sensemakr** for convergent credibility. - **Visualize**: always pair numerical tipping points with ggplot curves for interpretability. - **Document assumptions**: specify whether $γ_{UX}$ refers to log-OR, log-HR, etc. ## Conclusion *tipr* translates the abstract worry of “unmeasured confounding” into tangible numbers researchers can debate. Use the scaffolded examples above to build from single-scenario checks to fully automated robustness dashboards. ## References and Resources - tipr website and docs [R Causal](https://r-causal.github.io/tipr/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - McGowan LD (2022). *tipr: An R package for sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounders*. *JOSS*, 7 (77), 4495. DOI 10.21105/joss.04495 [Journal of Open Source Software](https://joss.theoj.org/papers/10.21105/joss.04495?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - CRAN manual (v1.0.2) [CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/tipr/tipr.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) - `tip_hr` documentation for HR correction details [RDocumentation](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/tipr/versions/1.0.2/topics/tip_hr?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
